text: Everything this chapter has covered so far — compliance inheritance, SOC 2 and ISO 27001 controls, the Azure and AWS tooling that scores and collects evidence — points toward one practical skill: actually getting ready for a real audit. The real difference between an easy audit and a painful one almost always comes down to when evidence gets gathered.

An audit runs on a fixed fieldwork window, during which an auditor reviews evidence and tests whether controls genuinely operate the way you say they do. Nearly everything they ask for falls into three buckets: configuration exports, like IAM policy or Azure RBAC role exports, encryption-at-rest settings, and the compliance reports Lesson 27's tools already generate; access logs, like CloudTrail or Azure Monitor Activity Log entries showing exactly who accessed what and when, retained long enough to cover the whole audit period; and policy documents, the actual written security and incident response policies that show day-to-day operations genuinely match what's on paper.

Two findings show up constantly in real cloud audits. Stale access is a permission still assigned after it's no longer needed — a departed employee's account never disabled, or an admin role granted for a one-time migration task and never revoked afterward. It's one of the single most common findings an auditor writes up, precisely because nobody's job is to notice forgotten access. Missing logging is the second: a resource with logging disabled outright, or retention set shorter than the audit period, leaving no evidence trail at all for the exact window an auditor needs to review.

Running a Compliance Manager assessment, assigning an Azure Policy regulatory compliance initiative, kicking off an Audit Manager assessment, or deploying a Config conformance pack weeks before fieldwork starts surfaces exactly these gaps — stale permissions, disabled logging, drifted encryption settings — while there's still time to actually fix them, instead of during the real audit.

That closes out compliance in the cloud. Chapter 8 starts the capstone: a hands-on lab setting up hybrid identity sync, bringing together everything from identity, zero trust, encryption, secrets, posture management, and now compliance into one end-to-end hybrid cloud environment.
